newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin sets French spending limits, awaits growth.
newsitem.headline: Jospin sets French spending limits, awaits growth.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will set next year's ministry spending limits on Friday but the crucial question for France's 1998 finances is whether economic growth will pick up soon enough to sort out his other problems.

Jospin increased the national minimum wage in July and is now hoping his efforts to stimulate consumer demand will bear fruit, improving tax and other state income to balance the budget without too much austerity on the spending side.

While many of his ministers enjoy a brief summer break after a hectic couple of months in power, Jospin is putting the seal on their individual budget allowances for 1998 and officials say the overall allocation will not be allowed to rise by more than two percent.

The officials say no details of the spending caps will be made public ahead of the completion of the 1998 budget bill for presentation to the cabinet on September 24. Ministers will receive their budget allocation letters from Jospin on August 12.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn revealed an audit of public finances on July 21 showing France's public deficit this year was heading for 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product -- well off the mark of three percent stipulated for joining European monetary union.

He announced a 32-billion-franc package of corporate tax hikes and savings to knock it down by about 0.4 percentage points and said the 1998 budget would be based on a strategy of ensuring a three percent deficit in 1998.

The dollar's rise of more than 20 percent against the franc may be welcome to the extent it helps export-based growth, but the jury is out on the extent to which consumer demand and business investment will provide a more lasting and widely-based pick-up in the economy.

Sonja Gibbs, economist at Nomura International bank, says the dollar's gains of close to 25 percent against the franc since January could theoretically add 0.2 or 0.3 percentage points to 1998 growth. But it is unclear current exchange rate levels will hold and rates used by the government in its forecasts are unknown, she said.

With moderate restraint on the ministry spending side, the next and hardest task facing the government is to work out the level of revenues it can depend on, at a time when record unemployment and relatively weak wage bill growth are weighing on tax revenues and social security contributions.
The previous centre-right government had forecast economic growth of at least 2.3 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent next year.
But some consider even these figures optimistic and many of the main monthly and quarterly economic indicators to date have proved inconclusive on the timing or likely strength of an upturn.

The government is still holding out hope of a pick-up and Strauss-Kahn says that if it came quickly and strongly enough, this year's finances could even register a deficit limited to three percent -- which would make the mathematics for 1998 easier as well.
